commentary.heading: US midterms whipsaw Wall Street
commentary.body: The Democrats' sweep of both houses of Congress first sparked a relief rally on Wednesday: the Dow gained about 3% and the S&P 500 1.6% as investors priced in less policy uncertainty and an earlier end to the Iran conflict, which sent Brent crude down roughly 8% to around US$95. The mood reversed on Thursday as investors dumped AI and chip stocks on fears a Democrat-led Congress will slow the data-centre build-out. The Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day since April 2025, closing in correction territory more than 10% below its 6 October record, while the S&P 500 lost 4.4% and the VIX volatility index jumped about 70%. Oil bounced 4% after tanker attacks in the Middle East.

commentary.heading: ASX: best day since April 2025, then a softer Friday
commentary.body: The ASX 200 rose 2.6% to 9,065 on Thursday, its strongest session since April 2025. Tech (+10%) led after NextDC surged 51% on stake-building by Goodman Group and Digital Realty, with miners up 7.6%; energy fell as oil slid. This morning the index opened about 1.2% lower in Wall Street's wake, a milder hit than elsewhere in Asia, where Korean and Taiwanese futures pointed to falls of 7% or more and Japan's almost 6%.

commentary.heading: Rates: the RBA and BoE tighten, the Fed waits
commentary.body: The RBA lifted the cash rate 25 bp to 4.85% on Tuesday, its fifth hike this year and the highest since 2008, after September CPI rose to 4.3% (trimmed mean 3.6%) on housing and fuel costs. A 6–3 vote and the removal of its tightening bias suggest a pause is likely at the 8 December meeting, and the Australian dollar slipped below 70 US cents. The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% on Thursday, its first hike since 2023, helping turn the FTSE 100 from a near-record intraday high to a 0.4% loss. The Fed held at 3.75–4.00% in October with two members wanting a hike; with US inflation at 3.7%, futures price a December increase.

commentary.heading: Bonds and the dollar
commentary.body: Yields eased as oil fell and investors sought safety: Australia's 10-year sits near 5.00%, a 10-week low, and the US 10-year around 4.88%, close to a two-month low. The Aussie dollar is around 69.3 US cents.

commentary.heading: China and Hong Kong
commentary.body: After the CSI 300's 8.5% slump in October, its worst month since 2016, Beijing's support signals (regulator meetings and PBOC liquidity) have steadied mainland shares; the Shanghai Composite was flat on Thursday near 3,690. The Hang Seng jumped 3.7% to a five-week high on tech before the US sell-off. Inflation remains subdued at 0.9% and the loan prime rate has been on hold at 3.00% for 17 months.

commentary.heading: What to watch
commentary.body: The US October jobs report (released early Saturday morning, Sydney time); Macquarie's half-year result today; whether the AI sell-off spreads further; China's October CPI on 9 November; and the next RBA (8 December) and Fed (December) decisions.
